Q: JS structuredClone: not truly deep copy? A:

On the contrary, the behaviour you're seeing PROVED it is a deep copy.

If you do the same assignment to the original object myObj, you will also observe:

myObj.field2[1] = 'baz'
console.log(myObj)
/**
{
    "field1": ["foo", "baz"],
    "field2": ["foo", "baz"],
    "field3": ["foo", "baz"],
}
**/

It is because the field values are referring to the same array object someSharedArray. When you try the same assignment to myObjCloned and observe the same outcome, it means the field values are referring to someSharedArray and the myObjCloned is the same as myObj, proving it's a deep clone.

If you expect to see this, that means it's NOT a deep copy.

/**
{
    "field1": ["foo", "bar"],
    "field2": ["foo", "baz"],
    "field3": ["foo", "bar"],
}
**/

I think the main confusion you had is not about structuredClone, but about object reference in JS.

Q: Define __dict__ in slotted dataclass A:

It's not entirely clear what you are trying to do here.

If you just want to get the existing fields of the dataclass in dictionary format, then you can use @robertspierre 's answer, or use dataclasses.asdict(). (Note that, if the value of any of the fields is another dataclass instance, asdict() will also recursively turn those into dicts too.)

If you want to actually give the dataclass a __dict__ member, so that you can add arbitrary members to the class's instances, well you can't do that using slots=True. You can, however, manually define slots for the class, and include __dict__, among them:

@dataclass()
class Circle:
    __slots__ = ('radius', '__dict__')
    radius: int = 2

Note that in this case, you will have to manually add each field to the slot list. Also note that circle.__dict__ will only contain those members that do not have their own slots, so you can't use it as a one-stop list of all the fields and their values.

(As for why anyone would want to do this? Well, there's a small speed advantage to accessing an instance member which is in a slot over one which is in __dict__. Also there is still potentially a memory advantage: adding __dict__ to __slots__ means instances can store arbitrary members in a dict, but Python is smart enough to only create that dict if and when it is actually needed, so any instances that only use the slotted members will have no dict and thus save memory.)

Q: Programmatic changes to input field on Swing and/or JavaFX, and preventing an infinite loop A:

Core Principle (Important)

Do not treat every text change the same.
User edits and programmatic updates must be distinguished at design level, not guessed later.

Approach 1: Guard / Flag Pattern (Most Common)

Use a boolean flag to suppress events during programmatic updates.

Concept:

  • User types → listener runs

  • Before updating field programmatically → disable listener

  • Update text

  • Re-enable listener

This prevents infinite loops and is widely used in both Swing and JavaFX.

Approach 2: Commit-Based Events (Better Architecture)

Instead of reacting to every text change:

  • React only when the user commits input
    (Enter key, focus lost, button click)

This way:

  • Backend updates never trigger user-input logic

  • Much cleaner event flow

Very common in professional UIs.

Approach 3: Property Binding with Source Control (JavaFX-style)

In JavaFX:

  • UI field is bound to a model

  • User updates model → backend call

  • Backend response updates model

  • UI reflects model automatically

Logic reacts to model changes, not raw text changes.

This avoids loops entirely when done correctly.

Approach 4: Temporarily Remove Listener

Before programmatic update:

  • Remove listener

  • Update text

  • Reattach listener

Works, but slightly heavier than flag approach.

Do one thing before you think, make sure you

  • Do not rely on timing

  • Do not compare old vs new text to guess intent

  • Do not allow backend updates to trigger user workflows

Treat user edits and backend updates as two different event paths. Use a guard flag or commit-based input handling so programmatic updates don’t re-trigger user listeners. This avoids infinite loops and keeps UI predictable.

Q: Installing Elasticsearch 6.8.15 on Apple-M1 Macbook issues A:

elasticsearch@6 is a homebrew-core package. It depends_on "openjdk", the jdk dependency is limited to openjdk distributed by homebrew-core as well. Installing JDK outside homebrew has not effect at all.

The problem is openjdk from homebrew-core had not been built for arm64 yet. But it seems when I answer the question, the openjdk has been supported.

brew install elasticsearch@6 should work now.

Extended Reading

For anyone looking for elasticsearch 7.x. Things haven't been changed in 2021.

Homebrew stops distributing newer version of elasticsearch, and kibana, although you can still get outdated versions in homebrew-core.

It's because Homebrew defers to the OSI's open source licence definition, and the new license used by elastic softwares is not compatible with it. So, elastic begins to distribute these software with its own custom tap.

# tap maintained by elastic organization
# https://github.com/elastic/homebrew-tap
brew tap elastic/tap

brew install elastic/tap/elasticsearch-full
# brew install elastic/tap/kibina-full
# brew install elastic/tap/logstash-full

Here's probably what you want to achieve:

- name: "Mysql Configuration - Resetting RootPassword"
  mysql_user:
    login_user: root
    login_password: actual_root_mysql_password
    host: ''
    name: root

Q: Auto Increment id in sharepoint A:

Use the title column to do this, not the ID.
In your workflow create a workflow variable type Integer. Then, add an action to calculate value using ID + 1000 and insert value into your variable.
Then, add action to concatenate Text + variable into Title field.
